narrative:
The model predicted a 56.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest factor and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Standing in only the second decile, far below the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among accepted students, signaled to the model that you might struggle with the demands of the bar exam. Your first-year ranking in the second decile reinforced this concern, though it carried less weight.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.20 worked in the opposite direction. Because it sits only slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted applicants, the model saw it as a modest positive signal that slightly increased the chance you would pass. Unfortunately, this encouraging nudge was not large enough to overcome the impact of your lower class rankings.

Given these results, you should focus on strengthening the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retaking key courses to improve your GPA, seeking academic support to raise your class standing, or gaining additional legal experience before reapplying could shift future predictions in your favor. Consider consulting an admissions advisor to identify the most effective steps for your next application cycle. (248 words)
